concepts.name: SI units, prefixes and homogeneity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Physical quantities as a number times a unit; the SI base quantities and units (kg, m, s, A, K and mol); derived units written as products and quotients of base units (N = kg m s⁻², J, W, Pa, C, V, Ω); checking that an equation is homogeneous (and why homogeneity does not prove an equation correct); the prefixes pico to tera and conversions between them, including area and volume units; standard form; making reasonable order-of-magnitude estimates of everyday quantities. Uncertainties are aphys.measurement.errors-uncertainties.

concepts.name: Errors, precision, accuracy and combining uncertainties
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Systematic errors (including zero errors) and random errors and how each is reduced; precision versus accuracy; absolute, fractional and percentage uncertainty; combining uncertainties by adding absolute uncertainties for sums and differences and percentage uncertainties for products, quotients and powers; quoting a result with its uncertainty to a sensible number of significant figures. Instrument use is aphys.measurement.instruments; uncertainty in a gradient is aphys.skills.data-analysis.

concepts.name: Scalars, vectors, adding and resolving vectors
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Scalar and vector quantities with examples from the syllabus; adding and subtracting coplanar vectors by scale drawing and by calculation (Pythagoras, sine and cosine rules); resolving a vector into two perpendicular components; resultant of forces at an angle; vectors on an inclined plane. Equilibrium vector triangles are aphys.forces.equilibrium.

concepts.name: Measuring instruments and the oscilloscope
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Choosing and reading instruments to their precision: metre rule, vernier and digital calipers, micrometer screw gauge (and zero error), top-pan balance, newton meter, stop-watch (timing many oscillations), protractor, thermometer, analogue and digital ammeters and voltmeters; using a cathode-ray oscilloscope (time-base and y-gain) to measure a p.d., a time interval and a frequency; light gates and data loggers for time, velocity and acceleration; calibration curves. Using the CRO for wave measurements is also met in aphys.waves.progressive-waves.

concepts.name: Displacement, velocity, acceleration and motion graphs
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Definitions of distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration; displacement-time and velocity-time graphs; velocity as the gradient of a displacement-time graph (tangents for curves); acceleration as the gradient of a velocity-time graph; displacement as the area under a velocity-time graph; sketching and interpreting graphs of journeys, including motion with changes of direction. The suvat equations are aphys.kinematics.suvat.

concepts.name: Equations of uniformly accelerated motion and free fall
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Deriving the equations of uniformly accelerated motion from the definitions and a velocity-time graph; solving problems in one dimension with consistent sign conventions; free fall in a uniform field without air resistance (g = 9.81 m s⁻²), objects thrown vertically; experiments to determine g (falling object timed with light gates or an electromagnet and trapdoor, and analysing s = ½gt² by a graph). Projectiles are aphys.kinematics.projectiles.

concepts.name: Projectile motion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Motion with a uniform velocity in one direction and a uniform acceleration perpendicular to it: independence of horizontal and vertical motion, horizontal launch and launch at an angle, time of flight, range, maximum height, velocity at any instant as a vector; qualitative effect of air resistance on the path. No calculus-based trajectory equations beyond the suvat equations.

concepts.name: Mass, weight and Newton's laws of motion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Mass as the property that resists change in motion; F = ma with acceleration in the direction of the resultant force; weight W = mg as the effect of a gravitational field on a mass; Newton's three laws stated and applied, including identifying Newton's third-law pairs correctly; free-body diagrams, connected bodies, lifts and inclined planes without friction coefficients. Momentum is aphys.dynamics.momentum-force.

concepts.name: Linear momentum and force as rate of change of momentum
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Linear momentum p = mv as a vector; force as the rate of change of momentum (F = Δp/Δt) and how F = ma follows for constant mass; impulse as change of momentum and the area under a force-time graph; applications such as crumple zones, catching, rockets and jets of fluid (qualitative to simple numerical). Conservation in collisions is aphys.dynamics.conservation-momentum.

concepts.name: Conservation of momentum and collisions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The principle of conservation of momentum for a closed system; elastic and inelastic collisions and explosions in one dimension and simple two-dimensional cases (components or a vector diagram); total kinetic energy conserved in an elastic collision and relative speed of approach equal to relative speed of separation; kinetic energy changes in inelastic interactions. Coefficient of restitution is out.

concepts.name: Friction, drag and terminal velocity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Qualitative frictional and viscous (drag) forces including air resistance; a simple model of drag increasing with speed; motion of a falling object with air resistance (acceleration decreasing from g to zero), terminal velocity, velocity-time graph shapes, parachutes and vehicles at top speed. No coefficients of friction or viscosity (Stokes' law out).

concepts.name: Centre of gravity, moments, couples and torque
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Centre of gravity as the point where the weight may be taken to act; moment of a force about a point (force × perpendicular distance); a couple as a pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces producing rotation only; torque of a couple (one force × perpendicular separation); simple applications such as steering wheels, spanners and beams. Equilibrium problems are aphys.forces.equilibrium.

concepts.name: Equilibrium of forces and the principle of moments
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The principle of moments; the two conditions for equilibrium (no resultant force and no resultant torque); coplanar forces in equilibrium represented by a closed vector triangle; solving problems with beams, ladders, hinged rods, suspended masses and three-force systems by moments, resolving and triangles of forces.

concepts.name: Density, pressure, hydrostatic pressure and upthrust
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Density ρ = m/V and pressure p = F/A; deriving and using p = ρgh for pressure in a fluid (and total pressure including atmospheric pressure); upthrust as the result of the difference in hydrostatic pressure on the top and bottom of an object; Archimedes' principle F = ρgV; floating and sinking, hydrometers and simple manometers. Fluid flow (Bernoulli) is aphys.matter.fluid-flow.

concepts.name: Work, conservation of energy and efficiency
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Work done as force × displacement in the direction of the force (including at an angle, W = Fs cos θ); energy transfers and the principle of conservation of energy; efficiency as useful energy output ÷ total energy input (as a ratio and a percentage); Sankey-style reasoning in words; problems combining work done against friction with energy changes. Power is aphys.energy.power; formulae for EP and EK are aphys.energy.gpe-ke.

concepts.name: Gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Deriving ΔEP = mgΔh from W = Fs in a uniform field and EK = ½mv² from the equations of motion; using both in problems with slopes, pendulums, roller coasters and falling objects, including energy lost to resistive forces. Gravitational potential energy in a radial field is aphys.gravitation.potential.

concepts.name: Power and P = Fv
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Power as work done (or energy transferred) per unit time, P = W/t; deriving P = Fv; power of vehicles at constant speed against resistive forces, lifting motors, pumps; efficiency combined with power (input and output power). Electrical power is aphys.electricity.pd-power.

concepts.name: Load, extension and Hooke's law
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Tensile and compressive forces and deformation in one dimension; load, extension, compression and limit of proportionality; Hooke's law and the spring constant k = F/x; force-extension graphs for springs, metal wires, rubber and polythene described in words and data; springs in series and parallel as an application (ZIMSEC detail to be confirmed; not required by Cambridge). Stress and strain are aphys.solids.stress-strain-young.

concepts.name: Stress, strain and the Young modulus
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Tensile stress σ = F/A, tensile strain ε = x/L and the Young modulus E = σ/ε; stress-strain graphs (gradient = Young modulus, ultimate tensile stress, breaking stress) for ductile and brittle materials; the experiment to determine the Young modulus of a metal wire (long wire, reference wire or marker and vernier, micrometer for diameter, plotting a graph, uncertainties).

concepts.name: Elastic and plastic deformation and strain energy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Elastic deformation, plastic deformation and the elastic limit; loading and unloading curves; the area under a force-extension graph as the work done; elastic potential energy EP = ½Fx = ½kx² within the limit of proportionality; energy stored per unit volume as an extension (ZIMSEC detail to be confirmed; not required by Cambridge); hysteresis in rubber described qualitatively.

concepts.name: Phases of matter and the kinetic molecular model
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Solids, liquids and gases described by a kinetic molecular model (spacing, ordering and motion of molecules); intermolecular forces and the variation of intermolecular potential energy and force with separation (described in words); explaining density differences between phases, melting, boiling and evaporation (and why evaporation cools) in molecular terms; Brownian motion as evidence for molecular motion; crystalline, amorphous and polymeric solids (ZIMSEC detail to be confirmed against the syllabus). Gas laws are aphys.gases.*; latent heat calculations are aphys.thermal.specific-heat-latent-heat.

concepts.name: Non-viscous fluid flow: continuity and Bernoulli
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Streamline (laminar) and turbulent flow; the ideal (non-viscous, incompressible) fluid; the continuity equation A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ as conservation of volume flow rate; Bernoulli's equation p + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline and its use in simple numerical problems; applications such as the Venturi meter, the aerofoil (lift), the spray atomiser, the filter pump and the Bunsen burner. Viscosity calculations are out. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Thermal conduction and thermal conductivity
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Conduction in solids by lattice vibrations and free electrons; temperature gradient; rate of heat flow through a slab Q/t = kA(θ₁ − θ₂)/x and the thermal conductivity k (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹); good and poor conductors; lagged and unlagged bars (temperature-distance graphs described in words); composite walls in series (equal heat flow rate) and insulation of buildings; Searle's bar and Lees' disc methods described in outline. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Convection and thermal radiation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Natural and forced convection explained by density changes; thermal radiation as electromagnetic (mainly infrared) radiation; emission and absorption by surfaces and the idealised black body; the Stefan-Boltzmann law P = σAT⁴ for a black body (net radiation σA(T⁴ − T₀⁴) as an extension); Wien's displacement law qualitatively (hotter bodies peak at shorter wavelength); applications: solar water heaters, vacuum flasks, greenhouses, cooling of electronic components. Stellar luminosity and radii are aphys.astro.*. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Thermal equilibrium and temperature scales
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Thermal energy flowing from higher to lower temperature; thermal equilibrium; thermometric properties (density of a liquid, volume of a gas at constant pressure, resistance of a metal, e.m.f. of a thermocouple) and how a scale is defined from fixed points; the thermodynamic (kelvin) scale as independent of any substance; absolute zero; T/K = θ/°C + 273.15; comparing liquid-in-glass, resistance and thermocouple thermometers (range, sensitivity, response time, remote reading).

concepts.name: Specific heat capacity and specific latent heat
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Defining and using specific heat capacity (ΔQ = mcΔθ) and specific latent heat of fusion and of vaporisation (ΔQ = mL); electrical methods to measure c of a metal block or a liquid and L of ice or water, with corrections for heat losses; method of mixtures; heating and cooling curves interpreted from data; energy and power problems (kettles, geysers, cooling of engines).

concepts.name: Internal energy and the first law of thermodynamics
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Internal energy as the sum of the random kinetic and potential energies of the molecules, determined by the state of the system; temperature rise linked to increase in internal energy (and phase changes to potential-energy change); work done W = pΔV when a gas changes volume at constant pressure, by and on the gas; the first law ΔU = q + W with the Cambridge sign convention (q = energy supplied by heating, W = work done on the system) and applying it to gas processes and phase changes. The ZIMSEC syllabus may use a different sign convention: confirm (ZIMSEC placement under 'Thermal properties of materials' is our mapping).

concepts.name: The mole and the ideal gas equation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Amount of substance as a base quantity (mol) and the Avogadro constant; an ideal gas as one obeying pV ∝ T; pV = nRT and pV = NkT with k = R/N_A; using the equation for fixed and changing amounts of gas, with temperatures in kelvin; the gas laws (Boyle, Charles, pressure law) as special cases and their experimental investigation; densities and number densities of gases. Kinetic theory is aphys.gases.kinetic-theory.

concepts.name: Kinetic theory of gases
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The basic assumptions of the kinetic theory; explaining gas pressure by molecular collisions; deriving pV = ⅓Nm⟨c²⟩ from a one-dimensional model extended to three dimensions using ⟨c²⟩ = 3⟨cₓ²⟩; mean-square and root-mean-square speed; comparing with pV = NkT to show that the mean translational kinetic energy of a molecule is (3/2)kT; molecular speeds of different gases at the same temperature.

concepts.name: Progressive waves: terms, wave equation and intensity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Wave motion in ropes, springs and ripple tanks; displacement, amplitude, phase difference (in degrees and radians), period, frequency, wavelength and speed; using the time-base and y-gain of a CRO to find frequency and amplitude; deriving and using v = fλ; energy transfer by progressive waves; intensity = power/area and intensity ∝ amplitude²; inverse-square fall of intensity from a point source as an application.

concepts.name: Transverse and longitudinal waves
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Comparing transverse and longitudinal waves (oscillation direction, examples: waves on strings and electromagnetic waves; sound); compressions and rarefactions; interpreting displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs of both kinds and converting a longitudinal displacement graph into positions of compressions and rarefactions; polarisation (qualitative) as evidence that a wave is transverse. Malus's law is aphys.waves.polarisation-malus.

concepts.name: The electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). All electromagnetic waves are transverse and travel at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ in free space; the principal regions from radio waves to gamma rays with approximate wavelength ranges (orders of magnitude only); visible light 400-700 nm; typical sources, detectors and uses of each region; calculations with c = fλ.

concepts.name: The Doppler effect for sound
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). The change in observed frequency when a source of sound moves relative to a stationary observer; explaining it with wavefront diagrams described in words; f_o = f_s v/(v ± v_s) for a moving source and stationary observer; applications (passing vehicles, sirens, speed measurement). A moving observer is out. Redshift of light is aphys.astro.redshift-hubble.

concepts.name: Polarisation and Malus's law
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). Plane polarisation as a property of transverse waves; polarising filters and polarised light (and microwaves with a metal grille); Malus's law I = I₀cos²θ for plane-polarised light passing through a polarising filter or a series of filters. The intensity change for unpolarised light entering a filter is out (Cambridge).

concepts.name: Superposition and stationary waves
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The principle of superposition; formation of stationary waves from two waves travelling in opposite directions (graphical method); nodes and antinodes; finding wavelength from node or antinode spacing (λ/2); stationary waves on stretched strings, in air columns (closed and open pipes, end corrections neglected) and with microwaves; harmonics and their frequencies; comparing stationary and progressive waves (energy, phase, amplitude).

concepts.name: Diffraction
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The meaning of diffraction; the effect of gap width (or obstacle size) relative to wavelength, demonstrated in a ripple tank and with sound, light and microwaves; why radio waves diffract round hills while light does not noticeably; diffraction as the reason two-source and grating patterns overlap. Single-slit intensity formulae are out.

concepts.name: Interference, coherence and the double slit
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Interference and coherence; conditions for observable two-source interference fringes (coherent sources, similar amplitudes, same polarisation for transverse waves); path difference and phase difference for constructive and destructive interference; demonstrations with water waves, sound, light and microwaves; Young's double-slit experiment and λ = ax/D, with measurement of fringe spacing over several fringes.

concepts.name: The diffraction grating
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). d sin θ = nλ; grating spacing from lines per millimetre; maximum order; sharper, brighter maxima than a double slit; determining the wavelength of light with a grating (spectrometer structure not required); spectra of white light and orders overlapping.

concepts.name: Electric current, charge and drift velocity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Current as a flow of charge carriers; charge is quantised (multiples of e); Q = It; the coulomb; current in metals, electrolytes and semiconductors; I = Anvq with number density n; drift velocity calculations and why it is small; comparing conductors, semiconductors and insulators by n.

concepts.name: Potential difference and electrical power
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Potential difference across a component as energy transferred per unit charge (V = W/Q); the volt; electrical power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; energy W = VIt and the kilowatt-hour; numerical problems on heaters, lamps, geysers and cables, including the cost of energy as simple arithmetic. E.m.f. is aphys.circuits.emf-internal-resistance.

concepts.name: Resistance, Ohm's law and I-V characteristics
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Resistance R = V/I and the ohm; Ohm's law and ohmic conductors; I-V characteristics of a metallic conductor at constant temperature, a filament lamp (resistance increases with temperature) and a semiconductor diode (forward and reverse bias, threshold about 0.6-0.7 V for silicon as a typical value); the LDR (resistance falls as light intensity rises) and the NTC thermistor (resistance falls as temperature rises); experiments to obtain characteristics. Resistivity is aphys.electricity.resistivity.

concepts.name: Resistivity
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). R = ρL/A and resistivity as a property of the material (Ω m); calculations with wires of different lengths and cross-sections (diameter measured with a micrometer); the experiment to measure the resistivity of a metal wire with a graph of R against L; typical orders of magnitude for metals, semiconductors and insulators; effect of temperature on resistance of metals in outline.

concepts.name: E.m.f., internal resistance and circuit symbols
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Circuit symbols and circuit diagrams (the Cambridge list); e.m.f. as energy transferred per unit charge in driving charge round a complete circuit; distinguishing e.m.f. and p.d. by energy; internal resistance, terminal p.d. V = E − Ir, lost volts; determining E and r from a graph of V against I; maximum power transfer as an extension (ZIMSEC detail to be confirmed; not required by Cambridge).

concepts.name: Kirchhoff's laws and resistors in series and parallel
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Kirchhoff's first law as conservation of charge and second law as conservation of energy; deriving R = R₁ + R₂ + … and 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + … from them; combined resistance of series-parallel networks; current and p.d. sharing. Multi-loop problems are aphys.circuits.kirchhoff-problems.

concepts.name: Solving circuits with Kirchhoff's laws
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Applying Kirchhoff's laws to networks with more than one source or several loops (simultaneous equations), with ammeters and voltmeters treated as ideal; effect of meter resistance as an extension; checking answers by energy balance.

concepts.name: Potential dividers and sensor circuits
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The principle of a potential divider and V_out = V_in R₂/(R₁ + R₂); variable output with a rheostat or a variable resistor; thermistors and LDRs in potential dividers giving a p.d. that depends on temperature or light intensity; loading effect of a connected meter or load; design reasoning for a simple sensor circuit (which resistor to place where).

concepts.name: The potentiometer and null methods
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). The slide-wire potentiometer as a means of comparing potential differences (balance length proportional to p.d.); using a galvanometer in null methods (no current at balance, so no p.d. lost across internal resistance); comparing e.m.f.s of cells and measuring internal resistance with a potentiometer; the Wheatstone bridge as a null method (ZIMSEC detail to be confirmed; not required by Cambridge).

concepts.name: The nuclear atom, nuclides and isotopes
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). The α-particle scattering experiment and what its results show (a small, dense, positively charged nucleus); a simple nuclear model with protons, neutrons and orbiting electrons; proton number and nucleon number; isotopes; nuclide notation; orders of magnitude of atomic and nuclear radii; the unified atomic mass unit u; conservation of nucleon number and charge in nuclear processes. Quarks are aphys.particles.quarks-leptons; energy levels are aphys.quantum.energy-levels-spectra.

concepts.name: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation and decay equations
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge AS Level). Composition, mass and charge of α, β⁻ (electron), β⁺ (positron) and γ radiation; their ionising and penetrating powers and deflection in fields; antiparticles (same mass, opposite charge; the positron); electron antineutrinos in β⁻ decay and neutrinos in β⁺ decay; discrete α energies versus the continuous β energy spectrum explained by the (anti)neutrino; balanced nuclear decay equations; background radiation and safe handling in outline. β⁺ decay and neutrinos are Cambridge detail (ZIMSEC coverage to be confirmed).

concepts.name: Quarks, hadrons and leptons
concepts.description: Cambridge only (AS Level). Quarks as fundamental particles with six flavours (up, down, strange, charm, top, bottom) and their charges; antiquarks; protons (uud) and neutrons (udd) as composite; hadrons as baryons (three quarks) or mesons (quark and antiquark); quark changes in β⁻ (d → u) and β⁺ (u → d) decay; electrons and neutrinos as leptons. No other quark properties (strangeness, colour) are required.

concepts.name: Radians and angular speed
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). The radian; angular displacement in radians and converting degrees to radians; angular speed ω; ω = 2π/T = 2πf and v = rω; examples with wheels, the Earth's rotation, CD-style discs and centrifuges.

concepts.name: Centripetal acceleration and force
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). A force of constant magnitude perpendicular to the velocity causes centripetal acceleration and uniform circular motion; a = rω² = v²/r; F = mrω² = mv²/r; identifying the force that provides the centripetal force (tension, friction, gravity, normal reaction, lift); horizontal circles, conical pendulum, banked tracks and vehicles over humps; vertical circles at top and bottom (tension or reaction). Orbits are aphys.gravitation.newtons-law-orbits.

concepts.name: Gravitational field and field strength
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). A gravitational field as a field of force; gravitational field strength g as force per unit mass; field lines for a point mass, a uniform sphere and near the Earth's surface; deriving g = GM/r² from Newton's law; using it for planets and moons; why g is approximately constant for small height changes near the Earth; variation of g with distance from the centre (outside the sphere). Newton's law itself is aphys.gravitation.newtons-law-orbits.

concepts.name: Newton's law of gravitation, orbits and geostationary satellites
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). A uniform sphere acts as a point mass at its centre for external points; Newton's law F = Gm₁m₂/r²; circular orbits with gravity providing the centripetal force (orbital speed, period, T² ∝ r³ derived for circular orbits); mass of a planet from a moon's orbit; geostationary orbits (24 h period, west to east, above the Equator) and their uses compared with low orbits.

concepts.name: Gravitational potential and potential energy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Gravitational potential at a point as the work done per unit mass bringing a small test mass from infinity; φ = −GM/r and why it is negative; gravitational potential energy E_P = −GMm/r of two point masses; changes in potential energy between orbits or heights; escape speed as an application (from ½mv² = GMm/r); field strength as the negative potential gradient in words.

concepts.name: Simple harmonic motion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Displacement, amplitude, period, frequency, angular frequency (ω = 2πf) and phase difference for oscillations; the defining condition a = −ω²x; x = x₀ sin ωt as a solution (and x₀ cos ωt); v = v₀ cos ωt and v = ±ω√(x₀² − x²); graphs of displacement, velocity and acceleration against time and against displacement; mass-spring and simple pendulum as examples with T = 2π√(m/k) and T = 2π√(l/g) used when given (the formulae are ZIMSEC detail to be confirmed; Cambridge gives them in context).

concepts.name: Energy in simple harmonic motion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). The interchange of kinetic and potential energy during s.h.m.; total energy E = ½mω²x₀²; kinetic and potential energy as functions of displacement and time described with data and in words; energy graphs.

concepts.name: Damped and forced oscillations and resonance
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Damping by resistive forces; light, critical and heavy damping and their displacement-time graphs; free and forced oscillations; resonance as maximum amplitude when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency; effect of damping on the resonance curve (lower, broader peak); useful and harmful resonance (radio tuning, microwave ovens, bridges, vehicle suspensions with critical damping).

concepts.name: Electric fields and uniform fields between plates
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). An electric field as a field of force; field strength as force per unit positive charge; F = qE; field lines (point charges, pairs of charges, parallel plates); the uniform field E = V/d between parallel plates; the motion of charged particles in a uniform field (acceleration parallel to the field, parabolic paths across it; energy gained qV); applications such as the electron gun and ink-jet deflection. Point charges are aphys.efields.coulomb-point-charge.

concepts.name: Coulomb's law and the field of a point charge
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). A charged conducting sphere acts as a point charge at its centre for external points; Coulomb's law F = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²) in free space; E = Q/(4πε₀r²); vector addition of fields and forces from two charges along a line or at right angles; comparing electric and gravitational forces (ratio for two protons or an electron and proton).

concepts.name: Electric potential and potential energy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Electric potential at a point as the work done per unit positive charge bringing a small test charge from infinity; V = Q/(4πε₀r); field strength as the negative of the potential gradient; electric potential energy E_P = Qq/(4πε₀r) of two point charges; equipotentials described in words; energy and closest-approach problems (α-particle and nucleus); analogies and differences with gravitational potential.

concepts.name: Capacitance and capacitor combinations
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Capacitance of an isolated spherical conductor and of a parallel-plate capacitor (defined as C = Q/V; C = 4πε₀r for an isolated sphere as a consequence); the farad and practical sizes; deriving and using formulae for capacitors in series and in parallel; charge and p.d. sharing in networks; uses of capacitors.

concepts.name: Energy stored in a capacitor
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Energy stored as the area under a p.d.-charge graph; W = ½QV = ½CV²= Q²/2C; energy delivered in camera flashes, defibrillators and backup supplies; energy lost when a capacitor is charged from a battery (half the energy supplied) as an extension.

concepts.name: Capacitor discharge and the time constant
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge A Level only). Graphs of p.d., charge and current against time for a capacitor discharging through a resistor; the time constant τ = RC; x = x₀e^(−t/RC) for current, charge or p.d.; time to halve; using ln graphs to find RC; charging curves described qualitatively (and quantitatively as ZIMSEC detail to be confirmed); smoothing link with aphys.ac.rectification-smoothing.

concepts.name: Magnetic fields and fields due to currents
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). A magnetic field as a field of force produced by moving charges or permanent magnets; field lines; field patterns of a long straight wire, a flat circular coil and a long solenoid, with direction rules; increase of field by a ferrous core; the forces between two current-carrying conductors (attract for parallel currents) explained and their directions determined; electromagnets and their uses. Formulae for B near a wire or in a solenoid are not required by Cambridge (ZIMSEC requirement to be confirmed).

concepts.name: Force on a current-carrying conductor and flux density
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, F = BIL sin θ; Fleming's left-hand rule; magnetic flux density B defined as force per unit current per unit length on a wire at right angles to the field; the tesla; current balance measurement of B; the d.c. motor principle and moving-coil meters as applications.

concepts.name: Force on moving charges, circular paths and velocity selection
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Direction of the force on a charge moving in a magnetic field; F = BQv sin θ; circular motion of a charged particle in a uniform field perpendicular to its velocity (r = mv/BQ); deflection of beams; velocity selection with crossed electric and magnetic fields (v = E/B); the mass spectrometer principle as an application. The Hall effect is aphys.magnetism.hall-effect; e/m experiments are aphys.particles.electron-charge-mass.

concepts.name: The Hall effect and the Hall probe
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). The origin of the Hall voltage when charge carriers in a current-carrying slice are deflected by a magnetic field; deriving and using V_H = BI/(ntq) with t the thickness; why the Hall voltage is larger in semiconductors (small n); using a Hall probe to measure magnetic flux density (orientation, calibration).

concepts.name: Charged particles: e, e/m and thermionic emission
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Thermionic emission and the production of electron beams; determination of the specific charge e/m of the electron by deflection in electric and magnetic fields (fine-beam tube or crossed fields), using eV = ½mv² and r = mv/Be; the principle of Millikan's oil-drop experiment as evidence for the quantisation of charge (balancing drops, E = V/d); the electronvolt. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus ('Charged particles'). Force on moving charges is aphys.magnetism.force-on-charge.

concepts.name: Magnetic flux, flux linkage and Faraday's law
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Magnetic flux Φ = BA (field perpendicular to the area; BA cos θ at an angle) and the weber; flux linkage NΦ; Faraday's law: induced e.m.f. equals the rate of change of flux linkage; calculations for a rod moving across a field (E = BLv), coils pushed into or rotated in fields, and changing currents; factors affecting the induced e.m.f. demonstrated by experiment. Lenz's law and applications are aphys.induction.lenz-applications.

concepts.name: Lenz's law and applications of induction
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Lenz's law as a consequence of conservation of energy; determining the direction of induced currents (Fleming's right-hand rule and Lenz); experiments with magnets falling through coils and tubes; eddy currents and magnetic braking; the a.c. generator principle (sinusoidal e.m.f. from a rotating coil, E₀ = BANω as an extension); back e.m.f. in motors in outline.

concepts.name: Alternating current: period, peak and r.m.s. values
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Period, frequency and peak value of an alternating current or voltage; x = x₀ sin ωt; root-mean-square values and I_rms = I₀/√2, V_rms = V₀/√2 for sinusoidal a.c.; mean power in a resistive load is half the peak power; reading a.c. waveforms on a CRO; mains voltages are quoted as r.m.s. values (50 Hz in Zimbabwe).

concepts.name: Rectification and smoothing
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Half-wave rectification with a single diode and full-wave rectification with a bridge of four diodes, with output graphs described; smoothing with a capacitor and the effect of the capacitance and the load resistance on the ripple (time constant compared with the period); the d.c. power supply as an application.

concepts.name: Transformers and power transmission
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). The principle of the iron-cored transformer (changing flux linkage in the secondary); the ideal transformer V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p = I_p/I_s; causes of energy losses (eddy currents, resistance of windings, hysteresis, flux leakage) and how laminations reduce them; efficiency; reasons for transmitting power at high voltage (I²R losses in cables) and the national grid with ZESA as context. Cambridge assumes IGCSE knowledge only. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Photons: energy, momentum and the electronvolt
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation; the photon as a quantum of energy; E = hf = hc/λ; the electronvolt and converting between eV and J; photon momentum p = E/c; photon numbers from power (number per second = P/hf).

concepts.name: The photoelectric effect
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Emission of photoelectrons from a metal surface by electromagnetic radiation; threshold frequency and threshold wavelength; work function; hf = Φ + ½mv²_max; stopping potential as an application; why maximum kinetic energy is independent of intensity but photoelectric current is proportional to intensity; why the wave model fails to explain the effect; graphs of E_k max against frequency (gradient h, intercept −Φ).

concepts.name: Wave-particle duality and electron diffraction
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). The photoelectric effect as evidence for particles, interference and diffraction as evidence for waves; electron diffraction through graphite as evidence for the wave nature of particles (qualitative interpretation of the rings); the de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; electrons accelerated through a p.d. (p = √(2meV)); comparing wavelengths with atomic spacings.

concepts.name: Energy levels and line spectra
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Discrete electron energy levels in isolated atoms (e.g. hydrogen), with energies given as negative values; excitation and ionisation; formation of emission and absorption line spectra; hf = E₁ − E₂; calculating wavelengths of spectral lines and identifying transitions; counting possible transitions.

concepts.name: Mass-energy equivalence, mass defect and binding energy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). E = mc² and the equivalence of mass and energy; nuclear equations such as ¹⁴N + ⁴He → ¹⁷O + ¹H; mass defect and binding energy (in J, MeV and u); binding energy per nucleon and the shape of its variation with nucleon number (peak near iron-56); calculating binding energies from masses in u (1 u ≈ 931.5 MeV as a stated conversion). Fission and fusion are aphys.nuclear.fission-fusion.

concepts.name: Nuclear fission and fusion
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Nuclear fission and fusion explained; the relevance of binding energy per nucleon to energy release in both; calculating the energy released from mass changes (ΔE = c²Δm); chain reactions, moderators and control rods in outline; fusion in stars and the conditions it needs (high temperature and density).

concepts.name: Radioactive decay: activity, decay constant and half-life
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Fluctuations in count rate as evidence of random decay; decay as spontaneous and random; activity A = λN; the becquerel; half-life; λ = 0.693/t½; exponential decay x = x₀e^(−λt) for activity, number of undecayed nuclei or count rate; correcting for background; ln graphs to find λ; carbon dating and medical/industrial isotope choice as applications.

concepts.name: Ultrasound: production, reflection and attenuation
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). The piezoelectric effect; generating and detecting ultrasound with a piezoelectric transducer; pulse-echo imaging and diagnostic information from reflections at tissue boundaries; specific acoustic impedance Z = ρc; intensity reflection coefficient I_R/I₀ = (Z₁ − Z₂)²/(Z₁ + Z₂)² and the need for a coupling gel; attenuation I = I₀e^(−μx); depth from echo time.

concepts.name: X-rays: production, imaging, attenuation and CT
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Production of X-rays by electron bombardment of a metal target; minimum wavelength from the accelerating p.d. (eV = hc/λ_min); X-ray imaging of internal structures and contrast (and contrast media); attenuation I = I₀e^(−μx) and half-value thickness; computed tomography: combining many X-ray images at different angles to build an image of a section, then repeating along an axis to build a 3D image.

concepts.name: PET scanning
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Radioactive tracers absorbed by the tissue studied; β⁺-emitting tracers in positron emission tomography; annihilation of a particle with its antiparticle with conservation of mass-energy and momentum; positron-electron annihilation producing two gamma photons travelling in opposite directions; energy of each photon (m_e c² ≈ 0.511 MeV); detecting the photons outside the body and building an image from arrival times.

concepts.name: Luminosity, radiant flux and standard candles
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Luminosity as the total power radiated by a star; the inverse-square law for radiant flux intensity F = L/(4πd²); standard candles (objects of known luminosity) and using them to find distances to galaxies; units (W, W m⁻², m and light-years as context, SI in calculations).

concepts.name: Wien's law, the Stefan-Boltzmann law and stellar radii
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Wien's displacement law λ_max ∝ 1/T to estimate the peak surface temperature of a star (constant given when needed); the Stefan-Boltzmann law L = 4πσr²T⁴; combining them to estimate stellar radii; comparing stars by temperature and size.

concepts.name: Redshift, Hubble's law and the Big Bang
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Increase in wavelength of spectral lines from distant galaxies; Δλ/λ ≈ Δf/f ≈ v/c for a source moving relative to an observer; redshift as evidence of an expanding Universe; Hubble's law v ≈ H₀d (SI units) and how it leads to the Big Bang theory; an estimate of the age of the Universe as 1/H₀ as an extension.

concepts.name: The operational amplifier: properties and comparator
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). The ideal operational amplifier: infinite open-loop gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance, infinite bandwidth, infinite slew rate (and real values in outline); inverting and non-inverting inputs; V_out = A₀(V⁺ − V⁻) and saturation at the supply voltages; the op-amp as a comparator with sensors (switching at a set temperature or light level) and LED or relay outputs. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Negative feedback, inverting and non-inverting amplifiers
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Negative feedback and its effects (reduced gain, increased bandwidth, stability); the virtual earth; inverting amplifier gain −R_f/R_in and non-inverting amplifier gain 1 + R_f/R₁; input and output voltage graphs, saturation; voltage follower; simple design calculations. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Sensors and output devices
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Sensing devices: LDR, thermistor, strain gauge (resistance change with strain), piezoelectric transducer, microphone; using them with potential dividers and op-amps to give a voltage output; calibration; output devices: relays (with a protective diode), LEDs (with series resistor) and calibrated analogue meters; a simple monitoring or control system described block by block. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Logic gates and truth tables
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Digital (two-state) signals; the NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR (and EXOR) gates with their symbols and truth tables; combining gates and working out truth tables of combinations; NAND and NOR as universal gates (building NOT, AND and OR). Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus (O-level logic gates are assumed known).

concepts.name: Combinational logic systems
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Designing a logic circuit from a written specification and its truth table (control and alarm systems with sensors as inputs); Boolean expressions for simple combinations; the half adder; the bistable (latch) as a one-bit memory described by its truth table as an extension. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Modulation: AM and FM
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). The principle of modulation and why a carrier wave is used; amplitude modulation and frequency modulation described with waveforms in words and data; sidebands and bandwidth (AM bandwidth 2f_m; FM frequency deviation in outline); comparing AM and FM (bandwidth, range, noise, cost); radio wavebands (LW, MW, VHF, UHF) in outline. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Analogue and digital signals, sampling and conversion
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Analogue and digital signals; advantages of digital transmission (regeneration, noise rejection, extra data); sampling, sampling rate (at least twice the highest frequency) and number of bits; analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue conversion with binary numbers; effect of sampling rate and bit depth on the reproduced signal; parallel-to-serial conversion in outline. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Communication channels, attenuation and decibels
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Form 6). Channels: wire pairs, coaxial cables, radio waves (surface, sky and space waves), microwave links, satellites (geostationary and polar orbits, uplink and downlink frequencies) and optical fibres; relative advantages (bandwidth, noise, cross-talk, security, attenuation); attenuation and amplification in decibels (10 lg(P₁/P₂)), signal-to-noise ratio, attenuation per unit length; the mobile phone network (cells, base stations, switching centre) in outline. Scope to be confirmed against the ZIMSEC syllabus.

concepts.name: Recording results, tables and graphs
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Practical skills of Cambridge Paper 3 and the ZIMSEC practical examination: setting up and collecting an appropriate range and number of readings, repeating readings; single results tables with quantity/unit headings and consistent precision of raw data; significant figures in calculated values (same as or one more than the least precise data); plotting graphs (scales, labels, points), lines of best fit and tangents; reading gradients (large triangle) and intercepts including with a false origin; relating y = mx + c to a physical equation to determine constants.

concepts.name: Uncertainties in readings, limitations and improvements
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 5; Cambridge AS Level). Estimating absolute uncertainty in a reading (instrument resolution, half the range of repeats); percentage uncertainty; testing whether data support a proportional relationship by comparing the percentage difference of a constant with a stated percentage uncertainty (Cambridge Paper 3 question 2); identifying the main limitations and sources of uncertainty in a method (quantity plus reason) and suggesting realistic improvements (not 'repeat readings' alone); predictions from data.

concepts.name: Planning an investigation
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Planning questions (Cambridge Paper 5 question 1; ZIMSEC practical planning to be confirmed): identifying independent, dependent and control variables; a workable method with a described labelled arrangement; how each variable is measured (instruments and precision), varied and kept constant; analysis (what graph to plot and how a constant follows from its gradient or intercept); safety precautions with reasons; additional detail such as preliminary experiments and calibration; use of oscilloscopes, light gates, data loggers and sensors.

concepts.name: Data analysis: linearising, logarithms, error bars and worst lines
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Form 6; Cambridge A Level only). Rearranging relationships into y = mx + c, y = axⁿ (lg y against lg x) and y = ae^(kx) (ln y against x); choosing derived quantities to plot; units in tables with logarithms (ln(d/cm)) and decimal places of logs; error bars from absolute uncertainties; the line of best fit and the worst acceptable line; uncertainty in a gradient and an intercept; determining a constant with its uncertainty and expressing it as value ± uncertainty with a unit (Cambridge Paper 5 question 2).
